clue.text: Confirm leaders of assembly securely bound…

indicators.note: the leaders of a pair of words are their opening letters, one taken from each

parts.note: bound, as in 'bound to happen', means sure or certain

explanation.surface: Someone checks that the heads of an assembly are firmly tied up.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm a fact is to establish it for sure, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: i.e. Charlie's bound over

indicators.note: bound here means enclosed or tied round, so Charlie surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a charlie is British slang for a fool, a twit; the 's means 'has'
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie has been bound over by the court, that is to say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound over' reads as a legal phrase, but 'bound' is the container signal and 'over' gives O.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation i.e. (id est) is read out as 'that is' or 'namely', an exact equivalent phrase.

clue.text: Person not likely to stand out, one part of the spectrum being diminished

definitions.text: Person not likely to stand out

parts.note: becoming smaller means shrinking
violet is one of the colours of the rainbow spectrum

explanation.surface: A shy person is compared to one colour band of the rainbow growing smaller.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrinking violet is an idiom for a very shy, retiring person who avoids attention.

clue.text: Rejected sole method of buying antiseptic

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: sole means single or lone
HP is hire purchase, the British instalment-buying scheme

explanation.surface: A turned-down way of paying in instalments for a disinfectant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' reverses LONE plus HP together, LONEHP becoming the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Phenol, also called carbolic acid, was the first widely used surgical antiseptic.

clue.text: Perspective shows sort of square in height or width, but not length

indicators.note: in places the square's letter inside what is left of the other word
but not means the following item is removed

parts.note: altitude is height; latitude (old sense: width) works as well, losing its L the same way
a T-square is a drawing tool, so T is a sort of square

explanation.surface: A point of view illustrated with a technical drawing square measuring height or width but not length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' drops L from ALTITUDE, leaving ATITUDE, and 'in' puts T inside after the first A. LATITUDE (width) minus L with T inserted gives the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An attitude is a way of looking at things, a viewpoint or outlook.

clue.text: Landlord with brains printed notepaper

parts.note: a landlord lets property, so is a letter
head means intelligence or brains

explanation.surface: A property owner with intelligence uses headed stationery.
explanation.walkthrough: LETTER is read as 'one who lets', a classic crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Letterhead is stationery printed at the top with a name and address.

clue.text: Doctor seen after morning rounds

indicators.note: seen after places the doctor's letters after the morning's

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for morning (ante meridiem)
MO is a medical officer, a doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor visits patients after the morning ward rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rounds' looks like a doctor's ward visits, but it means bullets.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is short for ammunition, and rounds are individual shots or cartridges.

clue.text: A few in public office put back targets

indicators.note: put back means the run of letters is read in reverse
a few letters inside the phrase are taken out as a run

explanation.surface: A small number in a government department are relegated to targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A few in' takes ICOF from 'public office' and 'put back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Foci, plural of focus, are centres of attention, so things aimed at, targets.

clue.text: CID staff possibly seal leak

parts.note: DIs, detective inspectors, are staff of the CID, Britain's plain-clothes police branch
a seal is a closure, something that closes

explanation.surface: Police detectives might seal off a leak of information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' marks DIS as an example of CID staff, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is an unauthorised disclosure, a revealing of secret information.

clue.text: Clubs less willing to admit single trader

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: to admit is to let something in, so the single letter goes inside

parts.note: loth means unwilling, so lother is less willing
I is the Roman numeral one, single

explanation.surface: A club that is more reluctant to let in an individual businessman.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothier is a merchant who makes or sells cloth or clothes.

clue.text: Achilles' carrier, a believer, is dropping back

indicators.note: dropping back moves the two letters to the end of the word

parts.note: a theist believes in God
taken as written

explanation.surface: Achilles' mother, a person of faith, falls behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping back' moves IS in THEIST to the end, giving THET plus IS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sea nymph Thetis was the mother of Achilles, so she carried him in the womb.

clue.text: Marianne, Carl, etc moving from the Isthmus

indicators.note: moving means the letters are shifted about into a new order

explanation.surface: Marianne, Carl and others move from the narrow land bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges all fifteen letters of MARIANNE, CARL and ETC.
explanation.definitionFit: Central America is the isthmus joining North and South America, so its people are from the Isthmus.

clue.text: Queen's favourite couple of characters granted audience

indicators.note: granted audience means heard, so the letters are taken by sound

parts.note: two letters of the alphabet, ess and ex, said together

explanation.surface: Elizabeth's courtier was allowed to speak to her in person.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the letter names 'ess' and 'ex' sound like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, was the famous favourite of Queen Elizabeth I.

clue.text: Well-meaning types leave after event, commissions having run out

indicators.note: after places the leaving word after the event word

parts.note: a do is a party, an event
to leave is to go

indicators.note: out means the run letter is put out of the word, removed

parts.note: commissions are orders placed
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Kindly people leave after the party, with their commissions expired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes R from ORDERS, leaving ODERS; 'having' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Do-gooders are earnest well-intentioned people, often regarded as naive.

clue.text: Author's written up main work

indicators.note: written up in a down clue means set upward, so read backwards

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the sea
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A writer's major work is written up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written up' turns only the sea word round, since this is a down clue; the 's of 'Author's' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek writer of fables, so an author.

clue.text: Tales in circulation that often attract little interest?

definitions.meaning: current means in circulation and accounts are stories, tales
bank accounts for day-to-day use pay little or no interest

explanation.walkthrough: 'interest' plays on attention versus money paid by a bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Current accounts are everyday British bank accounts; and stories doing the rounds are current accounts.

clue.text: Rehearses when the score's complete?

definitions.meaning: to go through something again in practice
read as runs plus over: in cricket, when the runs are over the scoring is finished

explanation.walkthrough: 'score' suggests music, fitting rehearsal, but the second reading is about runs being over.
explanation.definitionFit: To run over a piece is to rehearse or review it quickly.

clue.text: Alliance vehicles, first to leave

indicators.note: first to leave means the opening letter is taken away

parts.note: taxis are vehicles

explanation.surface: Coalition cars, the leading one departing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Axis was the Second World War alliance of Germany, Italy and Japan; an axis is an alliance between powers.

clue.text: Late worker or two from Edinburgh buried in dark church

indicators.note: buried in puts the Scottish word inside the other pieces

parts.note: dark, after nightfall, is night
twa is the Scots word for two

explanation.surface: A Scottish pair is buried in a gloomy church by a worker at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two from Edinburgh' points to the Scots dialect word for two; 'buried in' lodges it between the T of night and what precedes it. 'or' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A night watch is a guard kept overnight, or the person on it, so someone working late.

clue.text: Four or six in contest failing to finish? Matters very little

indicators.note: in places the Roman numeral inside the shortened word
failing to finish means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a trial is a contest or test
IV is four in Roman numerals; VI (six) inserted after TRI gives the same result

explanation.surface: A small number in an incomplete competition hardly matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to finish' cuts the last letter of the contest word, and 'in' inserts the numeral; four or six both work, which is why the clue offers either.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivia are trifles, things of very little importance.

clue.text: Carpenter's mate (male) to get rid of long hair

parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's poem the Walrus walks with the Carpenter
to get rid of is to oust
to long for is to ache for

explanation.surface: A carpenter's assistant wants to rid himself of his long hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long hair' seems a single phrase, but 'long' gives ACHE and 'hair' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A walrus moustache is a thick drooping growth of facial hair.

clue.text: Right turn, say, taken by Lear amongst others

parts.note: a title is a legal right, as in title to property
an actor's turn on stage is a role

explanation.surface: A rightward turn performed by Lear and others.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear plays the role named in the play's title, King Lear, as do Hamlet and Macbeth.

clue.text: Appearing badly dehydrated, she'll drive erratically

indicators.note: erratically means irregularly, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: She looks parched and will drive all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erratically' rearranges SHELL and DRIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrivelled means wrinkled and shrunken through loss of moisture.

clue.text: Jaques' speech describes this activity on ride

indicators.note: on in a down clue puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: life means liveliness or activity
to cycle is to ride a bike

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare speech describes busy goings-on during a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques gives the 'All the world's a stage' speech in As You Like It, tracing the seven ages of man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seven Ages speech traces a person's progression from birth to death.

clue.text: Casanova's flowing hair too long originally

indicators.note: originally means the first letter is taken
flowing means the letters move freely into a new order

explanation.surface: Casanova's flowing locks were rather too long at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowing' rearranges HAIR, TOO and L; 'Casanova's' means 'Casanova is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lothario, from Rowe's play The Fair Penitent, is a byword for a seducer, like Casanova.

clue.text: Middle section from The Thunderer getting chop in US..

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder
ax is the American spelling of axe

explanation.surface: A centre part from The Times, nicknamed The Thunderer, is cut in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thunderer is also a nickname for The Times newspaper, which misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: The thorax is the middle section of an insect's body, between head and abdomen.

clue.text: …passage from daily paper is lifted

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means raised up, so read backwards

parts.note: The Sun is a British daily tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A passage from a daily newspaper has been plagiarised.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to 18 down, whose subject is a newspaper; 'lifted' turns round both pieces together, and 'from' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is a cavity or channel in the body, such as a nasal passage.

clue.text: Superior stiffens up

indicators.note: up in a down clue means read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: gums means sticks or stiffens with gum

explanation.surface: A senior figure becomes rigid.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug means self-satisfied in a superior way.
